elements.quote: In this living systematic review and network meta-analysis we compare the effects of drug treatments for covid-19.
elements.reason: This sentence states the main objective and specifies the population/condition (covid-19) and the intervention type (drug treatments), matching the information conveyed in the title.

elements.quote: Living systematic review and network meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The phrase includes supplementary information about analysis method ('network meta-analysis') and update status ('living'), which are relevant supplementary details expected for the title.

elements.quote: Despite global efforts to identify effective interventions for the prevention and treatment of covid-19, which have resulted in approximately 3000 trials completed or underway, 2 evidence for effective treatment remains limited.
elements.reason: Text describes the current state of knowledge (large number of trials) and explicitly states that evidence for effective treatment remains limited, indicating important uncertainties.

elements.quote: Living systematic reviews deal with the main limitation of traditional reviews-that of providing an overview of the relevant evidence only at a specific time. 4 This is crucial in the context of covid-19, in which the best evidence is constantly changing. The ability of a living network meta-analysis to present a complete, broad, and updated view of the evidence makes it the best type of evidence synthesis to inform the development of practice recommendations.
elements.reason: The authors explain why a living network meta-analysis is needed (to address rapidly changing evidence and inform practice recommendations), establishing the importance and need for conducting this review.

elements.quote: To date, we are aware of two other similar efforts to ours. 42 43 Our intention is different in that the results fully inform clinical decision makingfor the associated living guidance. 6 Wealsoinclude a more comprehensive search for the evidence and several differences in analytical methods, which we believe are best suited for this evidence.
elements.reason: The authors acknowledge other similar systematic efforts and explain how and why the current review differs and is needed (different intention, more comprehensive search, different analytical methods).

elements.quote: Mounting evidence suggests that antivirals (such as molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir) are most effective in the early stages of covid-19 when patients have non-severe disease, whereas anti-inflammatories (such as corticosteroids) seem to be most effective in the later disease stages.
elements.reason: For interventions (drugs), the authors briefly describe differential proposed mechanisms/timing of effectiveness (antivirals early, anti-inflammatories later), addressing mechanism of action relevant to intervention effects.

No evidence in the provided material of a logic model or diagram showing hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes; nothing in retrieved evidence indicates a logic model was considered.

elements.quote: To compare the effects of treatments for coronavirus disease 2019 (covid-19).
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the review objective: to compare the effects of treatments for covid-19, which directly states the review question/objective.

elements.quote: Randomised clinical trials in which people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19 were randomised to drug treatment or to standard care or placebo.
elements.reason: For this intervention review, the planned comparisons are stated: the population is people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19 and the intervention/comparator contrast is drug treatment versus standard care or placebo (i.e., P and I and C are specified).

elements.quote: We included randomised clinical trials in people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19 that compared drugs for treatment against one another or against no intervention, placebo, or standard care. We included trials regardless of publication status (peer reviewed, in press, or preprint) or language. No restrictions were applied based on severity of illness or setting, and we included trials of Chinese medicines if the drug comprised one or more specific molecules with a defined molecular weight dosing. We excluded randomised trials evaluating vaccination, blood products and antibody-based antiviral therapies (such as virus-specific monoclonal antibodies), nutrition, traditional Chinese herbal or alternative medicines that include more than one molecule or a molecule without specific molecular weighted dosing, and non-drug supportive care interventions.
elements.reason: Specifies study design (randomised clinical trials), population (people with suspected/probable/confirmed covid-19), eligible comparisons (drugs vs drugs/no intervention/placebo/standard care), settings and severity (no restrictions), and explicit exclusions (vaccination, blood products, antibody therapies, non-drug interventions, complex herbal medicines).

elements.quote: We included trials regardless of publication status (peer reviewed, in press, or preprint) or language.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states inclusion regardless of publication status and language, but does not specify other report characteristics such as dissemination year; therefore reporting of report-characteristic criteria is only partial.

No explicit distinction was reported between excluding studies because outcomes were not measured versus excluding because outcome results were not reported; available evidence mentions trials with 'no outcomes of interest' but does not distinguish the two reasons.

elements.quote: For each outcome, interventions were classified in groups from the most to the least beneficial or harmful following GRADE guidance.
elements.reason: The methods state how interventions were grouped for the syntheses (classification into groups/nodes according to benefit/harm per GRADE). Additional evidence (callout_2 and text_26) documents node decisions (eg, combining placebo and standard care into the same node).

elements.quote: Many of the results for comparisons with sparse data were uninformative and were sometimes implausible. For that reason, we decided to report evidence on treatments for which at least 100 people were randomised or for which there were at least 20 events.
elements.reason: Provides a clear rationale for the notable restriction (analyzing only treatments with >=100 randomized people or >=20 events) due to sparse, uninformative, or implausible results.

elements.quote: The supplementary file includes the Chinese literature search strategy.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that the Chinese literature search strategy is provided in the supplementary file and that a protocol with detailed methods is available (text_12), but it does not present the complete search strategies as actually run for every database within the provided evidence. Therefore the requirement is only partially met.

elements.quote: We searched all English information sources from 1 December 2019 to 3 December 2021, and the Chinese literature from conception of the databases to 20 February 2021.
elements.reason: The report gives explicit date limits for English and Chinese searches and explains stopping Chinese database searches on 20 February 2021 because they had not provided studies that meaningfully altered the evidence (text_14), which describes and justifies search limits with reference to eligibility/utility.

elements.quote: We adapted the search terms for covid-19 developed by the CDC to the Chinese language.
elements.reason: The manuscript cites an existing (CDC) search approach and states that it was adapted for Chinese, satisfying the requirement to cite published search approaches/filters and describe adaptations.

No evidence that natural-language processing or text-analysis tools were used to identify or refine search terms; the only ML mention relates to filtering search results for randomized trials, not to developing search terms.
The evidence notes adaptation of search terms to Chinese but does not specify any tools used to translate search strings between sources.
The manuscript does not describe any validation of the search strategy itself (process or validation studies) in the provided evidence.
No description of any peer review of the search strategy (for example PRESS) is present in the provided evidence.

There is no information indicating whether the search structure was or was not based on PICO, nor any description of an alternative final conceptual structure; thus the conditional item is not addressed in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Usingasystematic review software, Covidence, 17 pairs of reviewers, followingtrainingandcalibrationexercises,independentlyscreened all titles and abstracts, followed by full texts of trials that were identified as potentially eligible. A third reviewer adjudicated conflicts.
elements.reason: States the number of reviewer pairs (17 pairs) who screened titles/abstracts and full texts, fulfilling the requirement to report number of reviewers per screening stage.

elements.quote: Reviewers resolved discrepancies by discussion and, when not possible, with adjudication by a third party.

No information reported about methods used to translate abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment in the supplied evidence.

elements.reason: Explicitly states that data were extracted by pairs of reviewers for each eligible trial.

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study. We used the number of patients ventilated at the time point that the largest number of the patients were ventilated, if the trial reported the number of patients ventilated at specific timepoints.
elements.reason: Provides explicit decision rules (a hierarchy) for selecting among reported measures for the mechanical ventilation outcome.

elements.quote: Selected outcomes included mortality (closest to 90 days), mechanical ventilation (total number of patients, over 90 days), adverse events leading to discontinuation (within 28 days), admission to hospital, length of hospital stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, and time to symptom resolution or clinical improvement.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the outcome domains sought and defines several (including mortality, mechanical ventilation, adverse events, admission, length of stay, duration of ventilation, and time to symptom resolution).

elements.quote: Selected outcomes included mortality (closest to 90 days), mechanical ventilation (total number of patients, over 90 days), adverse events leading to discontinuation (within 28 days)... In contrast to previous iterations, for this iteration, we did not include several outcomes which the GDG did not think were critical to decision making: viral clearance (closest to 7 days, 3 days either way), time to viral clearance, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, and days free from mechanical ventilation (within 28 days).
elements.reason: The time frame of measurement is specified for multiple outcome domains (e.g. mortality ~90 days, mechanical ventilation over 90 days, adverse events within 28 days, viral clearance ~7 days).

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study. We used the number of patients ventilated at the time point that the largest number of the patients were ventilated, if the trial reported the number of patients ventilated at specific timepoints.
elements.reason: The manuscript states selection rules for the mechanical ventilation outcome (a hierarchy) and describes general data collected, but does not explicitly state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought for every outcome domain.

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study. We used the number of patients ventilated at the time point that the largest number of the patients were ventilated, if the trial reported the number of patients ventilated at specific timepoints. We used author definitions for mechanical ventilation; when separate, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) were considered non-invasive mechanical ventilation.
elements.reason: When not all compatible results were sought (e.g. multiple time points or measures for mechanical ventilation), the manuscript describes the process/hierarchy used to select which results to collect and which definitions to apply.

elements.quote: In contrast to previous iterations, for this iteration, we did not include several outcomes which the GDG did not think were critical to decision making: viral clearance (closest to 7 days, 3 days either way), time to viral clearance, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, and days free from mechanical ventilation (within 28 days).
elements.reason: The manuscript reports changes to outcome-domain inclusion compared with previous iterations and provides the rationale (the guideline development group did not think these outcomes were critical).
No explicit statement was found describing changes to the processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains (i.e. any procedural changes over time) or rationales for such changes.

elements.quote: Outcomes of interest were selected based on importance to patients ... All panel members rated outcomes from 1 to 9 based on importance to individual patients (9 being most important), and we included any outcome rated 7 or higher by any panel member. Selected outcomes included mortality (closest to 90 days), mechanical ventilation (total number of patients, over 90 days), adverse events leading to discontinuation (within 28 days), admission to hospital, length of hospital stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, and time to symptom resolution or clinical improvement.
elements.reason: The manuscript states which outcomes were considered most important (those rated >=7 by panel members) and provides the rationale and process for prioritisation (patient importance ratings by the guideline panel).

elements.quote: Reviewers collected information on trial characteristics (trial registration, publication status, study status, design), patient characteristics (country, age, sex, smoking habits, comorbidities, setting and type of care, and severity of covid-19 symptoms for studies of treatment), and outcomesofinterest (means or medians and measures of variability for continuous outcomes and the number of participants analysed and the number of participants who experienced an event for dichotomous outcomes).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines multiple non-primary data items collected: trial characteristics, patient characteristics (with specific items), and outcome data types.

elements.quote: We used a hierarchy for the outcome mechanical ventilation in which we preferentially used the total number of patients who received mechanical ventilation over the study. We used the number of patients ventilated at the time point that the largest number of the patients were ventilated, if the trial reported the number of patients ventilated at specific timepoints. We used author definitions for mechanical ventilation; when separate, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) were considered non-invasive mechanical ventilation.
elements.reason: The authors describe explicit assumptions/decision rules for handling unclear or variably reported data (hierarchy for mechanical ventilation, use of author definitions, classification of CPAP/BiPAP).

elements.quote: For each eligible trial, pairs of reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, extracted data independently using a standardised, pilot tested data extraction form.
elements.reason: Although a standardised, pilot-tested data extraction form is mentioned, no specific tool or citation used to determine which data items to collect (e.g., a referenced checklist or established instrument) is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, used a revision of the Cochrane tool for assessing risk of bias in randomised trials (RoB 2.0)
elements.reason: The manuscript names the tool and version (a revision of Cochrane RoB 2.0) used to assess risk of bias.

elements.quote: across the following domains: bias arising from the randomisation process; bias owing to departures from the intended intervention; bias from missing outcome data; bias in measurement of the outcome; bias in selection of the reported results, including deviations from the registered protocol; bias due to competing risks; and bias arising from early termination for benefit.
elements.reason: The specific domains/components assessed by the risk-of-bias tool are explicitly listed.

elements.quote: We rated trials at high risk of bias overall if one or more domains were rated as probably high risk of bias or as high risk of bias and as low risk of bias if all domains were rated as probably low risk of bias or low risk of bias.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that an overall risk-of-bias judgement was made and specifies the rules used to derive the overall rating.

elements.quote: Risk of bias of the included studies was assessed using a modification of the Cochrane risk of bias 2.0 tool
elements.reason: The authors state they used a modification of RoB 2.0; supplementary text (text_17) further describes the domains used, indicating adaptations to the existing tool.
No evidence that a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created; the manuscript reports using a (modified) existing RoB 2.0 tool, so this item does not apply.

elements.quote: reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, used ... Reviewers resolved discrepancies by discussion and, when not possible, with adjudication by a third party.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes training/calibration and discrepancy resolution (discussion and third-party adjudication) but does not explicitly state how many reviewers assessed risk of bias per study or explicitly state that assessments were done independently.
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes to obtain/confirm risk-of-bias information from investigators.
There is no description of any automation tools used for risk-of-bias assessment, their use, training, performance, or validation.

elements.quote: We summarised the effect of interventions on dichotomous outcomes using the odds ratio and corresponding 95% credible interval. For continuous outcomes, we used the mean difference and corresponding 95% credible interval in days for ICU length of stay, length of hospital stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation because we expected similar durations across randomised trials. For time to symptom resolution, we first performed the analyses using the relative effect measure ratio of means and corresponding 95% credible interval before calculating the mean difference in days because we expected substantial variation between studies.
elements.reason: Specifies effect measures for dichotomous (odds ratio) and continuous outcomes (mean difference), and ratio of means for time to symptom resolution.

elements.quote: Judgments of imprecision for this systematic review were made using a minimally contextualised approach, with a null effect as the threshold of importance. ... To evaluate certainty of no benefit (or no effect), we used a 2% risk difference threshold of the 95% credible interval for mortality and mechanical ventilation. In other words, if the entire 95% credible interval was within 2% of the null effect, we would not rate down for imprecision. We decided on this preliminary threshold based on a survey of the authors.
elements.reason: Reports thresholds (null effect; 2% risk difference for mortality and mechanical ventilation) used to interpret effect size and explains rationale (survey of authors; minimally contextualised approach).

elements.quote: To facilitate interpretation of the results, we calculated absolute effects for outcomes in which the summary measure was an odds ratio or ratio of means. When available, we inferred baseline risk in the usual care group for each outcome from representative observational data (supplementary material). ... We calculated absolute effects using the transitive risks model 33 using R2jags package in R. 34
elements.reason: Describes method to re-express synthesized relative measures (odds ratios, ratio of means) as absolute effects using inferred baseline risks and the transitive risks model implemented with R2jags.

elements.quote: For continuous outcomes, we used the mean difference and corresponding 95% credible interval in days for ICU length of stay, length of hospital stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation because we expected similar durations across randomised trials. For time to symptom resolution, we first performed the analyses using the relative effect measure ratio of means and corresponding 95% credible interval before calculating the mean difference in days because we expected substantial variation between studies.
elements.reason: Provides justification for choice of effect measures: mean difference when durations expected similar, ratio of means when substantial variation between studies is expected.

elements.quote: Several trials could not be included in the analysis because both arms would have been classified within the same treatment node, they evaluated different durations or doses of the same drug, had insufficient data, or reported no outcomes of interest. Ultimately, we analysed 265 (63%) trials that reported on treatments with at least 100 patients or 20 events.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state the criteria and processes used to decide which trials were included in the synthesis (e.g. exclusion when arms fell in same node, differing doses/durations, insufficient data or no outcomes) and the a priori threshold for reporting (treatments with ≥100 patients or ≥20 events).

elements.quote:
Reviewers collected information on ... outcomes of interest (means or medians and measures of variability for continuous outcomes and the number of participants analysed and the number of participants who experienced an event for dichotomous outcomes). (text_16)

In the first iteration of this living network meta-analysis, some treatment nodes with few total participants and few total events resulted in highly implausible and extremely imprecise effect estimates. We therefore decided to include only treatments that included at least 100 patients or had at least 20 events, based on our impression of the minimum number of patients/events to possibly provide meaningful results. (text_21)
elements.reason: The manuscript reports aspects of data preparation: what summary statistics were collected (means/medians and measures of variability for continuous outcomes, counts for dichotomous outcomes) and a rule to exclude treatment nodes with very sparse data (minimum patients/events threshold). However, it does not describe explicit methods for handling missing summary statistics or any data conversions (for example, converting medians to means or imputing missing variances), so the reporting is incomplete for the checklist item.

elements.quote: All network meta-analyses were performed using the gemtc package of R version 3.6.3 (RStudio, Boston, MA) 26 and all pairwise meta-analyses using the bayesmeta package. 21
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports software packages and an R version used for statistical synthesis (gemtc in R v3.6.3) and the bayesmeta package for pairwise analyses.
No explicit description or justification of alternative synthesis or summary methods used when meta-analysis was not possible is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: As per our protocol, we used random effects for all outcomes. We used a plausible prior for variance parameter and a uniform prior for the effect parameter suggested in a previous study based on empirical data. 24
elements.reason: The manuscript states the model used (random-effects Bayesian framework for all outcomes) and provides a rationale (protocol decision; use of plausible priors informed by empirical study).

elements.quote: For most outcomes, we conducted network meta-analyses and pairwise meta-analyses using a bayesian framework with the same priors for the variance and effect parameters. ... For all analyses, we used three Markov chains with 100 000 iterations after an initial burn-in of 10 000 and a thinning of 10.
elements.reason: The statistical method is described: Bayesian network and pairwise meta-analyses with MCMC settings (chains, iterations, burn-in, thinning).

elements.quote: We used a plausible prior for variance parameter and a uniform prior for the effect parameter suggested in a previous study based on empirical data. 24
elements.reason: The manuscript reports use of a prior for the between-study variance (Bayesian approach) but does not report typical heterogeneity identification/quantification measures (for example I2 or explicit reporting of tau^2 estimates or formal heterogeneity tests) in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We used a plausible prior for variance parameter ...
elements.reason: For random-effects (Bayesian) analyses the manuscript specifies using a prior for the variance parameter (citing Turner et al.) but does not name a between-study variance estimator (frequentist estimator) — appropriate Bayesian prior is reported but no specific estimator is given.

elements.quote: All analyses reached convergence based on trace plots and a Brooks-Gelman-Rubin statistic less than 1.05, ...
elements.reason: The manuscript provides MCMC implementation details and elsewhere refers to 95% credible intervals; the use of Bayesian MCMC to generate credible intervals (posterior credible intervals) and convergence diagnostics is described, which addresses how interval estimates for the summary effect were calculated.

elements.quote: For all analyses, we used three Markov chains with 100 000 iterations after an initial burn-in of 10 000 and a thinning of 10. We used node splitting models to assess local incoherence and to obtain indirect estimates. 25
elements.reason: Other implementation details for the random-effects Bayesian analyses are provided: MCMC settings, node-splitting for incoherence, and use of specific packages.

elements.quote: We used a plausible prior for variance parameter and a uniform prior for the effect parameter suggested in a previous study based on empirical data. 24
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the prior distributions used for key quantities (variance and effect parameters) in the Bayesian analyses and cites the empirical source for these priors.
No methods describing how statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., correlated outcomes, multiple arms) were handled are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Mounting evidence suggests that antivirals (such as molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir) are most effective in the early stages of covid-19 when patients have non-severe disease, whereas anti-inflammatories (such as corticosteroids) seem to be most effective in the later disease stages. Therefore, going forward, we will perform separate living network meta-analyses for non-severe covid-19 and severe covid-19. Updates will continue to be published on covid19lnma.com.
elements.reason: The authors give an explicit plan for future work—performing separate living network meta-analyses for non-severe and severe COVID-19—constituting an explicit recommendation/action for future research.
